chapters.title: Investment Decisions: Capital Budgeting
chapters.summary: Relevant cash flows, payback, discounted payback, ARR, NPV, profitability index and IRR, NPV-IRR conflicts, and the basics of risk analysis in capital budgeting.

lesson.heading: Capital budgeting and relevant cash flows
lesson.body:
Capital budgeting is the process of evaluating long-term investment proposals (new plant, expansion, replacement, new products). The decisions involve large, mostly irreversible outlays whose benefits come over many years, so they must be judged on **incremental cash flows**, discounted at the **cost of capital**.

**Rules for relevant cash flows**

- Use cash flows, not accounting profit. **CFAT = PAT + Depreciation** = (EBDT - Depreciation)(1 - t) + Depreciation.
- Take only incremental flows. Ignore **sunk costs** (for example a feasibility study already paid for); include **opportunity costs** (for example rent forgone on a building used for the project).
- Ignore interest: financing cost is already in the discount rate.
- **Working capital** invested at the start is an outflow and is usually recovered at the end of the project's life.
- Include salvage value (net of tax effects where the question requires) in the final year.

| Stage | Items |
| --- | --- |
| Initial outflow (year 0) | Cost of asset + installation + working capital - sale value of old asset (replacement) |
| Operating inflows (years 1 to n) | CFAT = EBDT (1 - t) + Depreciation x t |
| Terminal inflow (year n) | Salvage value + recovery of working capital |

lesson.heading: Evaluation techniques
lesson.body:
| Technique | Formula / rule | Accept if | Main drawback |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Payback period | Years to recover outlay from CFAT | Below target period | Ignores time value and flows after payback |
| Discounted payback | Years to recover outlay from discounted CFAT | Below target period | Still ignores flows after payback |
| Accounting rate of return (ARR) | Average PAT / Average investment x 100; average investment = (cost - salvage)/2 + salvage + working capital | Above target rate | Uses profit, ignores time value |
| Net present value (NPV) | PV of inflows - PV of outflows | NPV > 0 | Needs a discount rate; absolute figure ignores scale |
| Profitability index (PI) | PV of inflows / PV of outflows | PI > 1 | Can conflict with NPV for mutually exclusive projects |
| Internal rate of return (IRR) | Rate at which NPV = 0 | IRR > cost of capital | Multiple IRRs for non-conventional flows; reinvestment assumption |

**IRR by interpolation**: find two rates, one giving a positive NPV and one a negative NPV, then

**IRR = L + [NPV at L / (NPV at L - NPV at H)] x (H - L)**

For equal annual inflows, compute the payback factor (outlay / annual CFAT) and find it in the annuity table between two rates.

**NPV vs IRR conflict** for mutually exclusive projects arises from differences in size, timing of cash flows or life. NPV assumes reinvestment at the cost of capital, IRR at the IRR itself. NPV is preferred because it measures the absolute addition to wealth.

lesson.heading: Risk analysis basics
lesson.body:
- **Risk-adjusted discount rate (RADR)**: discount at Rf + risk premium; riskier projects get higher rates.
- **Certainty equivalent (CE)**: multiply each expected cash flow by a CE coefficient (0 to 1) to get certain cash flows, then discount at the **risk-free rate**. Do not add a risk premium again.
- **Sensitivity analysis**: change one variable at a time (price, volume, cost, life, discount rate) and find the % change that makes NPV zero. Smaller % = more sensitive = riskier variable.
- **Scenario analysis**: NPV under worst, base and best combinations of variables.
- **Expected NPV and probability**: weight outcomes by probability; use standard deviation or coefficient of variation to compare risk.
- **Decision trees** for sequential decisions; **simulation** (Monte Carlo) for many uncertain variables.

lesson.heading: Worked example: payback, discounted payback, NPV and PI
Common mistakes
lesson.body:
- Deducting interest in CFAT. The discount rate already covers financing cost.
- Forgetting to recover working capital at the end, or to include it in the initial outlay.
- Adding the full depreciation charge to EBDT instead of the tax saving on it (CFAT = EBDT(1 - t) + Dep x t).
- Treating sunk costs as relevant.
- Ranking mutually exclusive projects of different size by PI or IRR when NPV gives a different answer. Use NPV.
- In the CE approach, discounting at the cost of capital instead of the risk-free rate (double counting risk).

keyPoints: CFAT = PAT + depreciation = EBDT(1 - t) + depreciation x t. Ignore interest and sunk costs; include opportunity costs.
Working capital is an outflow at the start and an inflow at the end.
ARR = average PAT / average investment; average investment = (cost - salvage)/2 + salvage + working capital.
NPV > 0, PI > 1, IRR > Ko: accept. NPV is preferred when methods conflict.
IRR = L + [NPV_L / (NPV_L - NPV_H)] x (H - L).
CE approach: CE coefficient x expected cash flow, discounted at the risk-free rate. RADR: discount at Rf + risk premium.

cases.title: Case: Tungabhadra Packaging Ltd
cases.body:
Tungabhadra Packaging Ltd is considering a new laminating machine.

- Cost ₹20,00,000; life 5 years; no salvage value; straight-line depreciation.
- Additional working capital of ₹2,00,000 is needed at the start and will be released at the end of year 5.
- Tax rate 25%; cost of capital 12%.

| Year | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Earnings before depreciation and tax (₹) | 6,00,000 | 7,00,000 | 8,00,000 | 8,00,000 | 6,00,000 |
| PV factor at 12% | 0.893 | 0.797 | 0.712 | 0.636 | 0.567 |

questions.prompt: Compute the payback period of the project (total outlay including working capital, CFAT including working capital release), in years to 2 decimals.
Compute the NPV of the project using the PV factors given (₹, nearest rupee).
The profitability index of the project (to 2 decimals) is:
questions.explanation: PI = PV of inflows / PV of outflows = 23,58,125 / 22,00,000 = **1.07**. 1.18 wrongly leaves working capital out of the outlay; 0.07 is NPV / outlay.

questions.prompt: The accounting rate of return on average investment is:
questions.explanation: Average PAT = (1,50,000 + 2,25,000 + 3,00,000 + 3,00,000 + 1,50,000) / 5 = 2,25,000. Average investment = 20,00,000/2 + 2,00,000 working capital = 12,00,000. ARR = 2,25,000 / 12,00,000 = **18.75%**. 11.25% uses the initial investment of 20,00,000 without working capital; 22.50% omits working capital from the average investment.

questions.prompt: What should Tungabhadra decide?
options: Accept: NPV is positive and PI exceeds 1
Reject: payback exceeds half the project's life
Reject: ARR is below the cost of capital plus tax
Accept only if the IRR is below 12%
questions.explanation: NPV of ₹1,58,125 means the project earns more than 12% and adds to shareholders' wealth. Payback is not a reason to reject a positive-NPV project unless a liquidity constraint is stated.

questions.prompt: The main reason NPV and IRR can rank mutually exclusive projects differently is that:
options: NPV assumes reinvestment of intermediate cash flows at the cost of capital, while IRR assumes reinvestment at the IRR
NPV ignores the time value of money
IRR uses accounting profit while NPV uses cash flows
IRR cannot be computed for projects with equal annual cash flows
questions.explanation: Differences in size, timing and life combined with different reinvestment assumptions cause conflicts. Reinvestment at the cost of capital is more realistic, so NPV is preferred.

questions.prompt: Under the certainty equivalent approach, the certainty-equivalent cash flows are discounted at:
options: The risk-free rate
The risk-adjusted discount rate
The firm's WACC plus a risk premium
The project's IRR
questions.explanation: The CE coefficients already remove risk from the cash flows. Discounting them at a risk-adjusted rate would count risk twice.

questions.prompt: A project costs ₹10,00,000 and gives CFAT of ₹3,00,000 a year for 5 years. The 5-year annuity factors are 3.352 at 15% and 3.274 at 16%. Compute the IRR by interpolation, as a % to 2 decimals.

A project costs ₹5,00,000. Expected CFAT is ₹3,00,000 in each of years 1 and 2, with certainty-equivalent coefficients of 0.9 and 0.8. Risk-free rate 6% (PV factors 0.943 and 0.890). Compute the NPV under the certainty equivalent approach (₹, nearest rupee; enter a negative number if negative).
The payback period method ignores cash flows that arise after the payback period.
questions.explanation: This is its main weakness along with ignoring time value. Discounted payback fixes the time value problem but still ignores later flows.

questions.prompt: Select all the discounted cash flow (DCF) techniques.
options: Net present value
Profitability index
Internal rate of return
Discounted payback period
Accounting rate of return
Simple payback period
questions.explanation: DCF techniques discount future cash flows. ARR uses accounting profit and simple payback ignores time value, so both are traditional (non-discounting) methods.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: profitability index = present value of cash inflows / present value of cash ___.
questions.explanation: PI > 1 means NPV > 0. PI is useful for ranking projects under capital rationing.

questions.prompt: A project costs ₹6,00,000 and yields CFAT of ₹2,00,000, ₹2,50,000, ₹2,50,000 and ₹1,50,000 over years 1 to 4. Cost of capital 10% (PV factors 0.909, 0.826, 0.751, 0.683). Compute the payback period, discounted payback period, NPV and profitability index.
Compare NPV and IRR. Which should be preferred when they give conflicting rankings for mutually exclusive projects?
questions.answer:
- NPV is the absolute surplus of PV of inflows over outflows at the cost of capital; IRR is the rate at which NPV is zero.
- For independent conventional projects both give the same accept/reject decision.
- For mutually exclusive projects they can conflict because of differences in initial outlay (size), timing of cash flows, or project life.
- NPV assumes reinvestment at the cost of capital; IRR assumes reinvestment at the IRR, which is often unrealistic.
- IRR can give multiple or no answers for non-conventional cash flows; NPV is additive across projects.
- NPV is preferred because it measures the actual increase in shareholders' wealth. Modified IRR can be used to remove the reinvestment problem.

questions.prompt: Explain the main techniques of risk analysis in capital budgeting.
questions.answer:
- Risk-adjusted discount rate: discount at the risk-free rate plus a premium that rises with project risk. Simple but assumes risk grows over time at a constant rate.
- Certainty equivalent: convert expected cash flows into certain ones using coefficients between 0 and 1 and discount at the risk-free rate. Separates time and risk, but coefficients are subjective.
- Sensitivity analysis: change one variable at a time and see the effect on NPV; identifies critical variables, but ignores interdependence.
- Scenario analysis: NPV under pessimistic, most likely and optimistic sets of variables.
- Probability approach: expected NPV, standard deviation and coefficient of variation.
- Decision trees for sequential decisions and Monte Carlo simulation for many uncertain variables.

chapters.title: Dividend Decision
chapters.summary: Relevance and irrelevance theories of dividend: Walter, Gordon, Modigliani-Miller, Graham-Dodd and Lintner models, with the factors that shape a firm's dividend policy.

lesson.heading: The dividend decision
lesson.body:
The dividend decision splits earnings between **payout** (dividend) and **retention** (reinvestment). Retention is the cheapest internal source of finance, so the decision is linked to the investment and financing decisions.

Two schools of thought:

- **Relevance theories** (Walter, Gordon, traditional Graham-Dodd): dividend policy affects the share price.
- **Irrelevance theory** (Modigliani-Miller): in perfect markets, value depends only on earning power and investment policy, not on how earnings are split.

Key terms: payout ratio = DPS / EPS; retention ratio b = 1 - payout; r = return on investment of retained earnings; Ke = shareholders' required return; g = b x r.

lesson.heading: Walter's model
lesson.body:
**P = [D + (r / Ke)(E - D)] / Ke**

where P = market price, D = DPS, E = EPS.

Assumptions: all financing through retained earnings (no new debt or equity), r and Ke constant, perpetual life, constant EPS and DPS.

| Type of firm | Condition | Optimal payout |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Growth | r > Ke | 0% (retain everything) |
| Normal | r = Ke | Irrelevant: any payout gives the same price |
| Declining | r < Ke | 100% (pay out everything) |

Example: E = ₹10, D = ₹4, Ke = 10%.

| r | Working | Price (₹) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 12% (growth) | [4 + 1.2 x 6] / 0.10 | 112.00 |
| 10% (normal) | [4 + 1.0 x 6] / 0.10 | 100.00 |
| 8% (declining) | [4 + 0.8 x 6] / 0.10 | 88.00 |

lesson.heading: Gordon's model and the bird-in-hand argument
lesson.body:
**P0 = E1 (1 - b) / (Ke - br)**, where br = g. It is the dividend growth model written in terms of retention.

Assumptions: all-equity firm, retained earnings the only source, r and Ke constant, Ke > br, perpetual life, no taxes.

Conclusions match Walter: retain more when r > Ke, pay out when r < Ke, irrelevant when r = Ke. The model breaks down if br ≥ Ke.

Gordon also argued (**bird-in-hand**) that investors are risk-averse and value a certain dividend today above uncertain future gains, so Ke rises as retention rises. On this view, dividends matter even for a normal firm.

lesson.heading: Modigliani-Miller, Graham-Dodd and Lintner
lesson.body:
**MM irrelevance**: P0 = (D1 + P1) / (1 + Ke). A dividend paid now reduces the year-end price by the same amount, so shareholders' wealth is unchanged. If the firm pays a dividend and still invests, it raises the shortfall by issuing new shares:

- Number of new shares Δn = [I - (E - nD1)] / P1
- Value of firm = [(n + Δn) P1 - I + E] / (1 + Ke), which is the same whatever the dividend.

Assumptions: perfect markets, no taxes or flotation costs, fixed investment policy, certainty. Criticisms: taxes, flotation costs, transaction costs, uncertainty and information content of dividends make dividends relevant in practice.

**Graham and Dodd (traditional)**: P = m (D + E/3), where m is a multiplier. Dividends get three times the weight of retained earnings.

**Lintner**: companies smooth dividends towards a target payout. D1 = D0 + [(EPS x target payout) - D0] x adjustment factor.

lesson.heading: Dividend policy in practice and common mistakes
lesson.body:
Factors: legal constraints (dividend only out of profits, as the Companies Act requires), liquidity, need for funds and growth opportunities, access to capital markets, stability of earnings, shareholder preferences and tax, lenders' covenants, inflation, and the signal a dividend change sends.

Forms: cash dividend, stock (bonus) dividend, share buy-back; policies: stable dividend per share, stable payout ratio, low regular plus extra.

**Common mistakes**

- Using r where Ke belongs in Walter's denominator. The outer division is by Ke.
- Using EPS instead of DPS in the numerator of Gordon's model.
- In MM, forgetting to compute P1 separately for "dividend" and "no dividend" cases.
- Applying Gordon when br ≥ Ke; the formula gives a meaningless or negative price.

keyPoints: Walter: P = [D + (r/Ke)(E - D)] / Ke. r > Ke retain all; r < Ke pay all; r = Ke irrelevant.
Gordon: P0 = E(1 - b) / (Ke - br); requires Ke > br. Bird-in-hand: certain dividends valued more.
MM: P0 = (D1 + P1)/(1 + Ke); new shares Δn = [I - (E - nD1)] / P1; firm value unchanged by dividend.
Graham-Dodd: P = m(D + E/3).
Lintner: D1 = D0 + (target payout x EPS - D0) x adjustment factor.
MM is criticised for ignoring taxes, flotation costs, transaction costs, uncertainty and information content.

cases.title: Case: Kaveri Chemicals Ltd
cases.body: Kaveri Chemicals Ltd has EPS of ₹20. Its shareholders require 12% (Ke) and the company earns 15% (r) on reinvested funds. The board is choosing between payout ratios of 20%, 50% and 100%. Assume the conditions of Walter's and Gordon's models hold.

questions.prompt: Using Walter's model, compute the market price per share at a 20% payout (₹, 2 decimals).
Using Gordon's model, compute the market price per share at a 50% payout (₹, 2 decimals). Take EPS of ₹20 as E1.
Under Walter's model, the optimal payout ratio for Kaveri is:
options: 0%, because r exceeds Ke
100%, because shareholders want cash
50%, because it balances growth and income
Any payout, because dividend policy is irrelevant
questions.explanation: Kaveri is a growth firm (r 15% > Ke 12%). Price rises as payout falls: ₹208.33 at 0%, ₹200 at 20%, ₹187.50 at 50%, ₹166.67 at 100%.

questions.prompt: Under Walter's model, the price at a 100% payout would be:
questions.explanation: With D = E = 20, the retention term is zero: P = 20 / 0.12 = ₹166.67. At 100% payout, every model reduces to E / Ke.

questions.prompt: If Kaveri could earn only 10% on reinvested funds, its optimal payout under Walter's model would be:
options: Indeterminate
questions.explanation: With r (10%) < Ke (12%), the firm is a declining firm; shareholders can earn more elsewhere, so paying out everything maximises price.

questions.prompt: According to Modigliani and Miller, dividend policy does not affect the value of the firm because:
options: A dividend paid now is exactly offset by a fall in the year-end share price, and any funding gap is filled by issuing new shares at a fair price
Investors always prefer capital gains to dividends
Dividends are taxed more heavily than capital gains
Firms with high payouts have lower cost of equity
questions.explanation: Under perfect markets, P0 = (D1 + P1)/(1 + Ke), so a higher D1 means a lower P1. Wealth depends only on earnings and investment policy.

questions.prompt: Under Gordon's model, for a growth firm (r > Ke), increasing the retention ratio will:
options: Increase the share price
Decrease the share price
Leave the share price unchanged
Make the share price infinite in all cases
questions.explanation: Reinvesting at r > Ke creates value, so a higher b raises P (as long as br stays below Ke).

questions.prompt: Using Lintner's model: last year's DPS was ₹4, current EPS is ₹12, the target payout ratio is 50% and the adjustment factor is 0.4. Compute the expected DPS (₹, 2 decimals).
questions.explanation: Target dividend = 12 x 50% = 6. D1 = 4 + (6 - 4) x 0.4 = 4 + 0.8 = **₹4.80**. Firms move only part of the way to the target, which smooths dividends.

questions.prompt: Using the Graham-Dodd model with a multiplier of 8, DPS of ₹6 and EPS of ₹15, compute the market price per share (₹).
Under Walter's model, the dividend payout ratio does not affect the share price of a firm whose return on investment equals its cost of equity.
questions.explanation: With r = Ke, the term r/Ke = 1 and P = [D + (E - D)] / Ke = E / Ke for every D.

questions.prompt: Select all assumptions of Walter's model.
options: All investment is financed by retained earnings only
The return on investment (r) and cost of equity (Ke) are constant
The firm has a perpetual life
The firm raises new debt every year to fund growth
Dividends are taxed at a higher rate than capital gains
questions.explanation: Walter assumes no external financing, constant r and Ke, constant EPS and DPS and a perpetual life. Taxes are ignored.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: Gordon's argument that investors value a certain dividend today more than uncertain future capital gains is called the bird-in-the-___ argument.
questions.explanation: "A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush." Risk-averse investors discount distant gains at a higher rate, so retention raises Ke.

questions.prompt: Ganga Ltd has 1,00,000 shares at ₹100 each. Ke is 10%. It expects net income of ₹10,00,000 and plans investment of ₹15,00,000 this year. It is considering a dividend of ₹5 per share at year-end. Using the MM model, compute (a) the year-end price with and without the dividend, (b) the number of new shares to be issued in each case, and (c) show that the value of the firm is the same.
questions.answer:
**(a) Year-end price**: P0 = (D1 + P1)/(1 + Ke), so P1 = P0(1 + Ke) - D1.

- With dividend: 100 x 1.10 - 5 = **₹105**
- Without dividend: 100 x 1.10 - 0 = **₹110**

**(b) New shares**

| Particulars | Dividend paid (₹) | No dividend (₹) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Investment required | 15,00,000 | 15,00,000 |
| Net income | 10,00,000 | 10,00,000 |
| Less: Dividend | (5,00,000) | Nil |
| Retained earnings | 5,00,000 | 10,00,000 |
| Amount to be raised | 10,00,000 | 5,00,000 |
| Price of new share (P1) | 105 | 110 |
| **New shares (Δn)** | **9,523.81** | **4,545.45** |

**(c) Value of the firm** = [(n + Δn)P1 - I + E] / (1 + Ke)

- With dividend: [(1,00,000 + 9,523.81) x 105 - 15,00,000 + 10,00,000] / 1.10 = (1,15,00,000 - 5,00,000) / 1.10 = **₹1,00,00,000**
- Without dividend: [(1,00,000 + 4,545.45) x 110 - 15,00,000 + 10,00,000] / 1.10 = (1,15,00,000 - 5,00,000) / 1.10 = **₹1,00,00,000**

The value is ₹1 crore either way, which proves MM's irrelevance proposition.

questions.prompt: State the Modigliani-Miller dividend irrelevance theory, its assumptions and its criticisms.
questions.answer:
- Theory: in perfect capital markets the value of a firm depends on its earning power and investment policy, not on its dividend policy. A dividend paid today lowers the ex-dividend price by the same amount; any funding gap is met by issuing new shares, so shareholders' wealth is unchanged.
- Formula: P0 = (D1 + P1)/(1 + Ke).
- Assumptions: perfect capital markets, rational investors, no taxes (or no difference between dividend and capital gains tax), no flotation or transaction costs, fixed investment policy, certainty about future profits.
- Criticisms: taxes differ between dividends and gains; flotation costs make external equity dearer than retained earnings; transaction costs make home-made dividends costly; under uncertainty dividends carry information (signalling); investors may prefer current income (bird-in-hand); markets are not perfect.

questions.prompt: Explain the factors that determine the dividend policy of a company.
questions.answer:
- Legal restrictions: dividend can be paid only out of profits as permitted by company law; lenders' covenants may limit payouts.
- Liquidity: profit may be tied up in assets; cash must be available.
- Investment opportunities and need for funds: growth firms retain more.
- Access to capital markets and cost of external funds.
- Stability of earnings: stable earnings support a stable dividend.
- Shareholders' expectations, tax position and the signal a change sends.
- Control: retention avoids dilution from new issues.
- Inflation and the need to replace assets at higher cost.

chapters.title: Management of Working Capital
chapters.summary: Operating cycle, estimation of working capital requirement, financing of working capital, and the management of cash, receivables, payables and inventory.

lesson.heading: Concepts and the operating cycle
lesson.body:
- **Gross working capital** = total current assets. **Net working capital** = current assets - current liabilities.
- **Permanent (fixed) working capital** is the minimum level always needed; **temporary (fluctuating)** working capital meets seasonal or peak needs.
- Too much working capital hurts profitability (idle funds); too little hurts liquidity. Managing it is a **risk-return trade-off**.

The **operating cycle** is the time from paying for raw materials to collecting cash from customers:

**Operating cycle = R + W + F + D - C**

| Component | Formula (days) |
| --- | --- |
| R: raw material storage period | Average RM stock / Average daily RM consumption |
| W: work-in-progress period | Average WIP / Average daily cost of production |
| F: finished goods storage period | Average FG stock / Average daily cost of goods sold |
| D: receivables collection period | Average receivables / Average daily credit sales |
| C: payables deferral period | Average payables / Average daily credit purchases |

Example: R 60, W 15, F 30, D 45, C 40 days gives an operating cycle of **110 days**. The number of cycles in a 360-day year is 360 / 110.

lesson.heading: Estimating working capital requirement
lesson.body:
ICAI questions give a cost sheet per unit, holding periods and credit periods, and ask for a statement of working capital. Two bases exist; follow the question.

- **Cash cost basis**: exclude depreciation (non-cash) and profit. Receivables are valued at cash cost of sales. This is the preferred basis because working capital finances cash costs.
- **Total cost / sales value basis**: receivables at cost of sales or at sales value if the question says so.

| Item | Valuation |
| --- | --- |
| Raw material stock | Months of RM holding x monthly RM consumption |
| Work-in-progress | Months x monthly production cost, with RM usually 100% and labour/overheads at stated % completion (often 50%) |
| Finished goods | Months x monthly cost of production (cash cost) |
| Receivables | Months x monthly cash cost of sales (or sales value if stated) |
| Cash | As given |
| Less: Payables for RM | Months of credit x monthly RM purchases |
| Less: Outstanding wages and overheads | Lag in months x monthly amount |
| Add: Contingency / safety margin | % as stated, on net working capital |

lesson.heading: Financing and managing the components
lesson.body:
**Financing approaches**

- **Matching (hedging)**: permanent needs from long-term funds, temporary needs from short-term funds.
- **Conservative**: long-term funds also cover part of temporary needs. Lower risk, lower return.
- **Aggressive**: short-term funds also finance part of permanent needs. Higher return, higher refinancing risk.

**Cash management**: prepare cash budgets; hold cash for transaction, precautionary and speculative motives. **Baumol model**: optimum cash = √(2 x U x P / S), where U = annual cash requirement, P = fixed cost per conversion of securities to cash, S = interest rate on securities. **Miller-Orr model**: cash moves randomly between a lower limit and an upper limit; when it hits either, it is restored to the **return point** (lower limit + spread / 3).

**Receivables management**: set credit standards, credit period, cash discount and collection policy. Evaluate a change in policy by incremental analysis: extra contribution minus extra bad debts, extra collection cost and the cost of funds tied up in extra receivables (at cost). **Factoring** transfers collection and, if without recourse, credit risk to the factor for a fee.

**Payables management**: use the full credit period, but compare the cost of forgoing a cash discount with the cost of borrowing.

**Inventory management**: **EOQ = √(2AO / C)**, where A = annual demand, O = ordering cost per order, C = carrying cost per unit per year. Use ABC analysis and set reorder levels and safety stock.

lesson.heading: Worked example: evaluating a change in credit policy
lesson.body:
Current credit sales ₹60 lakh on 30 days, bad debts 1%. Proposed: 60 days, sales ₹72 lakh, bad debts 2%. Variable cost 70% of sales; fixed costs ₹6 lakh (unchanged); required return 15%; 360-day year. Investment in receivables at total cost.

| Particulars (₹) | Present | Proposed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sales | 60,00,000 | 72,00,000 |
| Less: Variable cost | (42,00,000) | (50,40,000) |
| Less: Fixed cost | (6,00,000) | (6,00,000) |
| Less: Bad debts | (60,000) | (1,44,000) |
| Profit before cost of funds | 11,40,000 | 14,16,000 |
| Investment in receivables: total cost x days / 360 | 4,00,000 | 9,40,000 |
| Less: Cost of funds at 15% | (60,000) | (1,41,000) |
| **Net benefit** | **10,80,000** | **12,75,000** |

The proposed policy adds ₹1,95,000, so it should be adopted.

lesson.heading: Common mistakes
lesson.body:
- Including depreciation in working capital under the cash cost basis.
- Valuing receivables at sales value when the question asks for cash cost (profit is not a fund requirement).
- Valuing WIP at full cost when it is only partly complete.
- Deducting payables for wages or overheads computed on the wrong base (use the monthly amount x lag).
- In credit policy questions, computing the cost of funds on sales instead of cost, or forgetting that fixed costs do not change.
- Mixing 360 and 365-day years in one answer. Follow the question.

keyPoints: Gross WC = current assets; net WC = current assets - current liabilities.
Operating cycle = RM period + WIP period + FG period + receivables period - payables period.
Cash cost basis excludes depreciation and profit; receivables at cash cost of sales.
Matching approach: permanent WC from long-term funds, temporary WC from short-term funds.
Baumol: optimum cash = √(2UP/S). Miller-Orr: return point = lower limit + spread/3.
EOQ = √(2AO/C). Credit policy: compare incremental profit with cost of funds on extra receivables at cost.

cases.title: Case: Krishna Garments Ltd
cases.body:
Krishna Garments Ltd plans to produce and sell 1,20,000 units a year, evenly over 12 months. Cost and price per unit:

| Element | ₹ per unit |
| --- | --- |
| Raw material | 40 |
| Direct labour | 20 |
| Overheads (including depreciation ₹5) | 20 |
| Total cost | 80 |
| Profit | 20 |
| Selling price | 100 |

Other information:

- Raw material in stock: 1 month. Work-in-progress: 0.5 month (raw material 100% complete, labour and overheads 50% complete).
- Finished goods in stock: 1 month. Debtors: 2 months.
- Credit from RM suppliers: 1 month. Wages paid 0.5 month in arrears; overheads paid 1 month in arrears.
- Minimum cash balance: ₹1,00,000.
- Estimate working capital on a **cash cost basis** (exclude depreciation and profit; debtors at cash cost of sales).

questions.prompt: Compute the investment in work-in-progress (₹, nearest rupee).
questions.explanation: Monthly output = 10,000 units. WIP for 0.5 month = 5,000 units. Cost per unit of WIP = RM 40 + labour 20 x 50% + cash overheads 15 x 50% = 57.50. WIP = 5,000 x 57.50 = **₹2,87,500**.

questions.prompt: Compute the investment in debtors (₹, nearest rupee).
questions.explanation: Cash cost per unit = 40 + 20 + 15 = ₹75. Debtors = 2 months x 10,000 units x 75 = **₹15,00,000**. At sales value it would be ₹20,00,000, which wrongly includes profit and depreciation.

questions.prompt: Compute the net working capital requirement (₹, nearest rupee).
questions.explanation:
| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Raw material: 10,000 x 40 x 1 | 4,00,000 |
| Work-in-progress | 2,87,500 |
| Finished goods: 10,000 x 75 x 1 | 7,50,000 |
| Debtors: 10,000 x 75 x 2 | 15,00,000 |
| Cash | 1,00,000 |
| **Current assets (A)** | **30,37,500** |
| Creditors for RM: 10,000 x 40 x 1 | 4,00,000 |
| Outstanding wages: 10,000 x 20 x 0.5 | 1,00,000 |
| Outstanding overheads: 10,000 x 15 x 1 | 1,50,000 |
| **Current liabilities (B)** | **6,50,000** |
| **Net working capital (A - B)** | **23,87,500** |

questions.prompt: Why is the overhead of ₹20 per unit taken as ₹15 in the estimate?
options: Depreciation of ₹5 is a non-cash cost and does not need working capital funds
Overheads are paid one month in arrears
Only 75% of overheads relate to production
Overheads are recovered from customers in advance
questions.explanation: Working capital finances cash spent before cash is collected. Depreciation involves no cash outflow, so the cash cost basis excludes it.

questions.prompt: The amount of trade creditors for raw material in Krishna's estimate is:
questions.explanation: Monthly RM purchases (equal to consumption when stock levels are constant) = 10,000 x 40 = ₹4,00,000; 1 month's credit = ₹4,00,000. ₹6,50,000 is total current liabilities.

questions.prompt: Annual demand is 10,000 units, ordering cost is ₹200 per order and carrying cost is ₹4 per unit per year. The economic order quantity is:
options: 1,000 units
707 units
1,414 units
500 units
questions.explanation: EOQ = √(2 x 10,000 x 200 / 4) = √10,00,000 = **1,000 units**. 707 units drops the 2 from the formula; 1,414 units uses a carrying cost of ₹2.

questions.prompt: In the Baumol model of cash management, the optimum cash balance increases when:
options: The fixed cost per conversion of securities into cash rises
The interest rate on marketable securities rises
Annual cash requirement falls
The firm moves to a conservative financing policy
questions.explanation: Optimum cash = √(2UP/S). A higher P (conversion cost) means fewer, larger conversions, so a larger balance. A higher S makes holding cash costlier and lowers it.

questions.prompt: Under the matching (hedging) approach to financing working capital:
options: Permanent working capital is financed by long-term funds and temporary working capital by short-term funds
All working capital is financed by short-term bank borrowing
All working capital is financed by long-term funds
Temporary working capital is financed by equity
questions.explanation: Matching the maturity of funds with the life of the assets avoids both idle long-term funds and refinancing risk. The conservative approach uses more long-term funds; the aggressive approach uses more short-term funds.

questions.prompt: From the following annual data (360-day year), compute the operating cycle in days, to 1 decimal: average RM stock ₹3,00,000, RM consumed ₹24,00,000; average WIP ₹1,50,000, cost of production ₹36,00,000; average FG ₹4,50,000, cost of goods sold ₹45,00,000; average debtors ₹7,50,000, credit sales ₹54,00,000; average creditors ₹2,50,000, credit purchases ₹24,00,000.
Permanent working capital should ideally be financed from long-term sources.
questions.explanation: The permanent component is needed all the time, like a fixed asset, so financing it with short-term funds creates constant refinancing risk.

questions.prompt: Select all items that lengthen the operating cycle, other things being equal.
options: Longer raw material storage period
Longer receivables collection period
Longer finished goods storage period
Longer credit period obtained from suppliers
Faster conversion of WIP into finished goods
questions.explanation: R, W, F and D add to the cycle; C (supplier credit) is deducted, so longer supplier credit shortens it. Faster WIP conversion shortens W.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: in the Miller-Orr cash management model, when cash reaches the upper or lower limit it is brought back to the ___ point.
questions.explanation: Return point = lower limit + spread / 3. At the upper limit the firm buys securities; at the lower limit it sells them.

questions.prompt: Evaluate whether Sutlej Ltd should relax its credit policy. Show your working in the ICAI format.
questions.data:
- Present: credit sales ₹60,00,000, credit period 30 days, bad debts 1% of sales.
- Proposed: credit period 60 days, credit sales ₹72,00,000, bad debts 2% of sales.
- Variable cost 70% of sales; fixed costs ₹6,00,000 a year under both policies.
- Required pre-tax return on investment in receivables 15%. Ignore tax. Use a 360-day year and value receivables at total cost.
questions.answer:
| Particulars (₹) | Present policy | Proposed policy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Credit sales | 60,00,000 | 72,00,000 |
| Less: Variable cost (70%) | (42,00,000) | (50,40,000) |
| Less: Fixed cost | (6,00,000) | (6,00,000) |
| Less: Bad debts | (60,000) | (1,44,000) |
| (A) Profit | 11,40,000 | 14,16,000 |
| Total cost | 48,00,000 | 56,40,000 |
| Investment in receivables (total cost x days / 360) | 48,00,000 x 30/360 = 4,00,000 | 56,40,000 x 60/360 = 9,40,000 |
| (B) Cost of funds at 15% | 60,000 | 1,41,000 |
| **Net benefit (A - B)** | **10,80,000** | **12,75,000** |

**Decision**: the proposed policy increases the net benefit by ₹1,95,000 (12,75,000 - 10,80,000). Sutlej Ltd should extend the credit period to 60 days.

questions.prompt: Explain the factors that determine the working capital requirement of a business.
questions.answer:
- Nature of business: trading and manufacturing firms need more than service firms or utilities.
- Length of the operating (production) cycle: longer cycles need more working capital.
- Scale of operations and growth: expanding sales need more inventory and receivables.
- Seasonality: seasonal industries need large temporary working capital.
- Credit policy towards customers and credit available from suppliers.
- Market and demand conditions (inventory needed to meet competition), and price level changes (inflation raises requirement).
- Operating efficiency: faster inventory and receivables turnover reduce the requirement.
- Availability and cost of short-term finance and dividend/ retention policy.

questions.prompt: What is factoring? Explain its types and benefits to a business.
questions.answer:
- Factoring is the sale of book debts (receivables) to a factor, who advances a large part of their value, collects them and manages the sales ledger for a fee.
- Recourse factoring: the seller bears bad debts. Non-recourse factoring: the factor bears the credit risk, at a higher fee.
- Other forms: advance (factor pays upfront) vs maturity factoring (pays on due date), disclosed vs undisclosed, domestic vs export factoring.
- Benefits: immediate cash, lower investment in receivables, savings in collection and credit administration costs, protection from bad debts (non-recourse), and management time freed for core activities.
- Evaluation: compare the factor's commission and interest with savings in bad debts, administration costs and the cost of funds tied up in receivables.
